title: Anthropic's Claude autonomously discovers CRISPR-like enzyme system in bacteriophages
subtitle: A 21-hour agent campaign screening 200,000 reverse transcriptases surfaced a novel three-part biological system — the first published result from Anthropic's new life sciences lab.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic disclosed on September 23 that Claude agents flagged a previously uncharacterized enzyme system in bacteriophage DNA — the first published result from the life sciences research group the company stood up in the spring. The system, called array-associated reverse transcriptases or ART, has three parts working together: a reverse transcriptase, a partner gene next to it, and a long array of evenly spaced DNA repeats whose pattern resembles CRISPR arrays. The autonomous campaign ran for about 21 hours across 949 agent sessions and consumed roughly 216 million tokens. Agents screened more than 200,000 reverse transcriptases, narrowed the field to about 3,500 candidates, and produced 20 detailed reports. A preprint has been posted; peer review has not happened yet.

The result matters less because ART is confirmed useful — Anthropic explicitly says it does not yet know what the system does — and more because of what the campaign shows about agent-driven biology. Individual pieces of the ART system were already visible in public sequence databases. What was new was Claude flagging the enzyme plus the partner gene plus the repeat array as one coordinated unit and asking, in effect, why they were sitting together. Feng Zhang, one of the original CRISPR researchers at MIT, called it 'an exciting example of how AI agents can contribute to biological discovery.'

The context matters. Anthropic's life sciences group runs at biosafety levels 1 and 2 and does not handle human pathogens, and the company framed the disclosure carefully — a discovery, not a product. That posture is a departure from the usual model-release news cycle: no benchmark chart, no pricing table, no marketing push. It also lands at a moment when frontier labs are trying to prove that agentic research is worth the compute it consumes, and 'Claude found something a human missed in a database everyone had access to' is a cleaner narrative than most.

Takeaway for learners: the interesting engineering here is not the model — it is the harness. Nine hundred agent sessions coordinating across a public database is a pipeline problem, not a prompt problem. If you want to work on agent-native science, the skills that pay off are the boring ones: writing evaluation loops, deduplicating results, structuring outputs so a second agent can act on them. The model is the cheap part.
